lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand the sources, roles and effects of the following hormones: adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, progesterone and oestrogen

primer.text: You know hormones are blood-borne chemical messengers. This note profiles the five on the specification: adrenaline the emergency mobiliser, insulin the glucose balancer, and the three reproductive hormones testosterone, progesterone and oestrogen. For each, file three facts — source gland, role, and the effects it produces in target organs.

modules.title: Adrenaline and insulin
modules.opening: Adrenaline is the fight-or-flight hormone: danger triggers it, and it floods the body with preparations for movement — faster heart and breathing, redirected blood, widened muscle vessels, and stored glycogen broken into glucose. Insulin is its daily-life counterpart: the pancreas secretes it when glucose runs high, and muscles and liver stash the surplus as glycogen.
keyPoints: Adrenaline, produced in danger situations, readies the body for fight or flight.
Its effects include faster heart and breathing rates and blood flow redirected to muscles.
Adrenaline also widens muscle blood vessels and prompts stored glycogen to break into glucose.
Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood glucose when it climbs too high.
Muscles and liver take up the excess glucose and store it as glycogen until levels normalise.

low.restatement: Adrenaline mobilises: heart up, breath up, blood rerouted, glycogen split. Insulin stores: glucose taken in by liver and muscles, packed as glycogen.
low.analogy: Adrenaline rings the fire bell and opens every exit; insulin is the steward who calmly herds everyone back inside afterwards.
low.examPointer: For each hormone give source, role and effect — the table's three columns — never the role alone.

medium.restatement: Both hormones act by changing target-organ activity: adrenaline multiplies muscle fuel delivery for emergencies, while insulin closes the glucose loop that keeps concentration inside its narrow homeostatic band.
medium.analogy: One is an accelerator pressed to the floor; the other is the cruise control that quietly trims the speed back.
medium.examPointer: Insulin's story is a negative-feedback loop — detection by pancreas, secretion, uptake, normalisation, secretion stops. Recount it in that order.

modules.title: Testosterone and progesterone
modules.opening: Two more hormones, two different theatres. Testosterone comes from the male testes and builds the male reproductive system plus its secondary sexual characteristics — facial and underarm hair, a deepening voice, extra muscle mass. Progesterone comes from the ovaries and guards pregnancy: it maintains the uterine lining and blocks further ovulation.
keyPoints: Testosterone is produced in the male testes.
It drives growth of the male reproductive organs and the male secondary sexual characteristics.
Male characteristics named include facial or underarm hair, deeper voice and greater muscle mass.
Progesterone is produced in the female ovaries.
It holds the uterine lining in place through pregnancy while further ovulation is shut down.

low.restatement: Testes make testosterone (male development); ovaries make progesterone (pregnancy maintenance, ovulation blocked).
low.analogy: Testosterone is the builder of a second-stage renovation; progesterone is the caretaker who locks the doors once tenants move in.
low.examPointer: Attach the sex and the organ: testes-testosterone, ovaries-progesterone — source marks are free marks.

medium.restatement: Both are ovarian-or-testicular steroid messengers whose effects are sustained developmental or maintenance programmes rather than minute-to-minute adjustments.
medium.analogy: They are building codes, not traffic lights — long-term instructions shaping structure rather than daily traffic.
medium.examPointer: Progesterone's dual action earns two marks: maintains the lining AND prevents further ovulation.

modules.title: Oestrogen and the hormone summary
modules.opening: Oestrogen, from the ovaries, carries a double brief. It drives female secondary sexual characteristics — breast development, wider hips, pubic and underarm hair — and it regulates the menstrual cycle by stimulating repair of the uterus lining after menstruation while steering egg release through its influence on FSH and LH.
keyPoints: Oestrogen is produced by the female ovaries.
It develops female secondary sexual characteristics.
Named characteristics include breast development, wider hips and pubic or underarm hair.
It stimulates repair of the uterus lining after menstruation.
It steers egg release through its influence on other hormones, FSH and LH included.

low.restatement: Ovaries make oestrogen: it shapes female characteristics, rebuilds the lining each cycle, and steers egg release via FSH and LH.
low.analogy: Oestrogen is the renovation manager — redecorating the room (lining) while coordinating the delivery schedule (egg release).
low.examPointer: Quote both briefs in cycle questions: characteristic development AND cycle regulation — half answers lose half marks.

medium.restatement: Oestrogen's cycle role is coordination through influence: by acting on the pituitary hormones it times the repair-and-release sequence rather than doing either job directly.
medium.analogy: It is the conductor who cues the orchestra's sections, playing no instrument itself.
medium.examPointer: Remember the summary table's five rows — adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, progesterone, oestrogen — each with source, role, effect.

glossary.definition: The fight-or-flight hormone that speeds heart and breathing, reroutes blood and mobilises glucose in danger.
The pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose by driving uptake and glycogen storage.
A storage polymer of glucose kept in the liver and muscles.
The ovarian hormone developing female characteristics and steering the menstrual cycle.
